text: Body size is a fundamental biological trait that influences physiology, behavior, and ecology across all levels of biological organization (e.g., [ 1 – 4 ]). Dwarfism is one drastic form of body size shift, where isolation plays a key role, such as on islands [ 5 , 6 ]. The Island rule predicts that insular populations may shift toward dwarfism (or gigantism) in response to novel ecological conditions such as resource availability, competition, and predation [ 7 ]. Dwarfism may confer energetic advantages by reducing maintenance costs, improving heat exchange, and facilitating earlier reproduction [ 8 , 9 ]. In high-elevation or cold-climate systems, similar constraints on body size can arise from short growing seasons and extreme climate regimes [ 8 , 9 ]. Under such conditions, environmental isolation can act analogously to geographic isolation by restricting dispersal and reinforcing local adaptation. Genetic isolation can also drive dwarfism, often in association with reduced genetic diversity of the founding population (founder effect) and subsequent divergence via genetic drift [ 10 ]. Whether environmental or genetic, isolation is key to dwarfism because of its potential to release populations from traditional selection pressures while concurrently subjecting these populations to novel selective pressures and increased exposure to the effects of genetic drift or inbreeding [ 11 ].
